articles.title: Here’s the Science Behind the Sunday Scaries—And How to Banish Them So You Can Actually Enjoy Your Entire Weekend
articles.content:
It usually starts with one seemingly simple thought. Tomorrow is Monday.
One minute, you’re enjoying the last stretch of your weekend. The next, you’re mentally opening your inbox, rehearsing tomorrow’s meeting in your head and remembering those three things you swore you would deal with on Friday and somehow never got to. Your shoulders tense. Your stomach twists. The weekend was supposed to last until you were nestled in bed, but your brain is already sounding Monday morning’s alarm clock.
That familiar shift from relaxed to vaguely doomed is what people mean when they talk about the Sunday scaries. And if you’ve ever Googled “what are the Sunday scaries” while actively experiencing them, you’re far from alone.
In a 2025 survey by Adobe of 1,004 full-time U.S. employees, 82% said they had experienced the Sunday scaries. And it gets worse: 42% said they had lost sleep over them, and 35% reported physical symptoms such as headaches, tension and fatigue.
Despite the cute alliterative name, there is real science behind the feeling. And believe it or not, it’s not all bad news. In fact, Alexander J. Shackman, PhD, a University of Maryland psychology professor who studies fear and anxiety, says mild Sunday nerves may even be useful. “They’re a chance to take stock of the successes and failures of the recent past, size up the most important challenges in the week to come and plan accordingly,” he explains. The trouble begins when that preparation system stops helping and starts hijacking your day.
So how do you get your brain to cut that out? We’ve got the answer, of course! Read on to find out what’s going on when you get that telltale twinge of anxiety on Sundays—and how to combat it.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more science, life, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
The Sunday scaries are the dread, worry or uneasiness that can show up as your time off winds down and the next workweek gets closer. You might feel restless, irritable or distracted. Your thoughts may race through Monday’s schedule, and you may have trouble relaxing or falling asleep.
Why Sunday? Shackman says part of the answer may be contrast. Saturday is the weekend’s peak, baby! You’re riding the high of that Friday feeling, and you’re safely removed from work. On the other end of the spectrum, once you’ve hit Tuesday, you are already back in the rhythm of the week. Sunday sits at the uncomfortable border between weekend freedom and whatever responsibilities are waiting on the other side.
“It feels like you’re about to encounter something different, something potentially stressful or challenging,” he says. Your brain notices that shift and starts preparing.
Anxiety is partly a preparation system. It pulls your attention toward possible problems so you can respond to them. That’s useful when there’s something concrete to prepare for, such as a deadline, presentation or difficult conversation.
Some weeks simply give that system more material. In Adobe’s 2025 survey, burnout was the most commonly reported trigger, cited by 55% of respondents. High workloads came next at 50%, followed by project deadlines and toxic work environments.
The response can also change, depending on how threatening a situation seems and whether you feel equipped to handle it. Shackman says the brain takes into account things like how likely a problem is and what options you have for coping with it. When the response becomes much bigger than the actual demands, it’s like an overly sensitive security system. Instead of helping you prepare, it keeps sounding the alarm.
There is no tiny “Monday” switch in your brain. Anticipating a possible threat recruits a network of interconnected regions that work together to prepare your mind and body.
In a 2025 study published in the Journal of Neuroscience and co-authored by Shackman, researchers used fMRI scans to study threat anticipation in 220 adults. Both certain and uncertain threats engaged a shared network that included the extended amygdala, anterior insula and midcingulate cortex. Here’s how it all breaks down.
The extended amygdala, located at the base of the forebrain, includes structures involved in organizing responses to danger. In the study, this area remained more persistently active when people anticipated an uncertain threat.
That helps explain why something that has not happened yet can still feel urgent. Your brain does not have to wait for Monday morning to start monitoring what might go wrong.
Shackman says parts of the prefrontal cortex are also involved in anticipating stress. This area helps with planning, decision-making and regulating behavior.
That can turn worry into useful action. You check your calendar, decide what needs your attention and move on. The problem is when planning turns into rumination and you keep circling the same fears without solving anything.
The anterior insula and midcingulate cortex are also part of the threat-anticipation network identified in Shackman’s study. Together, these regions help your brain prioritize potentially important information.
“Emotionally charged stimuli—pain, threat, dangers and so on—hijack attention,” Shackman says. Helpful when actual danger is nearby. Less helpful when you are trying to enjoy your Sunday and your mind is already at work.
Once your brain senses a challenge, the response can spread through your body. Stress activates systems that affect heart rate, blood pressure and stress hormones. In a 2022 study published in Psychophysiology, researchers randomly assigned 99 people to a stressful task or a control condition. The stress group showed higher cardiovascular responses, including changes in heart rate and blood pressure.
Your body can also react before the stressful event begins. A 2022 study published in Biological Psychology measured cortisol in 78 college students on a regular class day and on the day of an exam. About 37% showed a specifically anticipatory response, with cortisol peaking before the exam rather than afterward.
Sleep can take a hit too, according to other studies. That is one reason Sunday-night worrying can be so frustrating. You are trying to prepare for Monday while potentially making yourself more tired for it.
First, ask whether the anxiety is actually helping. If a few minutes of thinking about Monday leads to a plan and you feel better afterward, the system may be doing its job. If you routinely wake up on Sundays with your mind racing, cannot enjoy the day or lose sleep over work, Shackman says the response is no longer helping you prepare.
Sometimes the issue is not your coping strategy. “For some people, escaping the Sunday scaries might require looking for a new job or renegotiating the current one,” Shackman says. “After all, some jobs really are terrible.” If the anxiety is intense, persistent or interfering with your life, it is also worth talking with a health-care or mental-health professional.
Don’t worry—we have a plan! These tips will help you get your end-of-the-weekend anxiety under control.
Give yourself a short window to look at the week ahead, decide what actually needs your attention and write it down. Then stop. One recent study found that emotionally loaded work rumination was associated with greater fatigue, while problem-solving thoughts were not. A specific plan may help you move from repeatedly worrying about work to deciding what you can actually do about it.
If Sunday becomes one long period of mentally preparing for work, you never really get the recovery part of the weekend. A 2022 study found that among Japanese teachers who entered the weekend with higher stress, greater weekend relaxation was associated with a larger reduction in psychological stress. Translation: Do something that actually feels restorative to you and treat it as part of the weekend, not time you should be using to get ahead.
Shackman’s advice is refreshingly uncomplicated. “Go for a walk or, better yet, a run. Lift some weights. Sign up for a class at the gym or YMCA,” he suggests.
Exercise is not a universal cure, but it gives you something concrete to do with that restless energy and can help you shift your attention away from the worry loop. You don’t need a heroic workout either. The goal is to interrupt the pattern, not add another item to your list of things you failed to accomplish this weekend.
Give work thoughts a stopping point, especially if checking your inbox tends to generate five new things to worry about. The sleep research matters here because anticipating stress can affect sleep even before the stressful event occurs.
A little anticipation can be useful. But when your brain starts treating Monday like an emergency before Sunday is even over, the goal is not to eliminate every worried thought—it’s to give yourself enough space to prepare, then let the rest of the weekend belong to you.

We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. For this piece on the Sunday scaries, Miranda Manier tapped her longtime experience as a journalist and health editor to ensure that all information is accurate and offers the best possible advice to readers. articles.title: Don’t Throw Away That Old Phone! Here’s How to Turn It into a Free Security Camera
articles.content:
Chances are, you’re holding on to an old iPhone or a cracked Android tablet you haven’t used in … let’s just say a really long time. Maybe you think it could come in handy, especially if your new device ever goes on the fritz, or that it could be worth money someday. Or maybe you just don’t know how to dispose of it properly. All legit reasons, even as the tech clutter keeps (and keeps) accumulating.
Well, we have some good news for you: Your time has finally come—and you’re about to save a bundle with this clever upcycling hack. I have turned old devices into everything from digital photo frames to oversized TV remotes, but my favorite trick, by far, is turning them into security cameras. You can put them in a nursery like a baby monitor, watch your pets while you’re at the office or even prop them up on windowsills to keep an eye on your packages.
It works like a charm, just like a pricey Nest camera—except it’s free. It’s also super easy to set up, as long as you have a clear set of instructions.
Read on to find out how to do it, plus some tips for making sure your old tech is secure.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more tech, travel, cleaning, humor and fun facts all week long.
Apps can breathe new life into older hardware, whether you have a spare iPhone, iPad or Android. Essentially, you download an app to both your old device and the smartphone or tablet you use every day. This turns your old device into the “camera” and your everyday gadget into the “viewer.”
Place your old device where you want in your home, connect it to Wi-Fi and plug it into the wall for power. And that’s it!
There are a few “free security camera” apps I’ve tried over the years, but some were too difficult to use or not really free. I eventually found Alfred Camera, which I think is the best all-around choice. And yes, I use it in my own home. While there’s a premium (read: paid) option with extra features starting around $36 per year, you can get a lot out of the free, ad-supported version.
If you want to see your camera feed from a desktop computer, use the Alfred Camera WebViewer. And yes, it’s free too!
Pretty much! As long as you can download the app, it works with all makes and models of older phones and tablets.
Yes. Aside from the fact that you will see ads in the free version, there are also a few restrictions:
But hey, free is free!
Buying an indoor Wi-Fi security camera could cost you anywhere from $25 to $150. And beyond that, there are the cloud service fees for recording and accessing the footage, which could run you $40 to $200 per year. So, yes, this old-device trick is quite the deal.
There are always privacy and security concerns when running apps, but that’s especially true on an older device, says Iskander Sanchez-Rola, senior director of AI and Innovation at Norton, a leading cybersecurity company. “If a new security flaw is discovered, an unsupported phone may never get the fix,” he cautions. “Before repurposing an old phone or tablet, check whether it’s still receiving security updates.”
It’s also important to remember that your old device may also contain loads of sensitive data about you that you may have forgotten about. “If you never wiped it, the device may still contain personal information from when you used it before,” Sanchez-Rola says. “So if the phone itself were ever compromised, both the camera feed and other personal data on the device could potentially be exposed.”
Plus, there’s something to consider about “free” apps: They are usually monetized in other ways. It could be advertisements, but also check to see if an app is using or sharing your data in any way. Sanchez-Rola says to start with the app store itself. On Apple devices, go to the app you’re interested in and look at “App Privacy” to see what it says; on Android, check “Data safety.” Sanchez-Rola says to “skim the privacy policy for terms like advertising, tracking, sharing and third parties. Think of the privacy label as the nutrition label, and the privacy policy as the ingredients list. Check both.”
Just remember that these disclosures are based on information provided by the developer. “They’re useful,” says Sanchez-Rola, “but they’re not an independent audit of everything the app is doing.”

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more tech, travel, cleaning, humor and fun facts all week long.

How does this work, exactly?

Apps can breathe new life into older hardware, whether you have a spare iPhone, iPad or Android. Essentially, you download an app to both your old device and the smartphone or tablet you use every day. This turns your old device into the “camera” and your everyday gadget into the “viewer.”

Place your old device where you want in your home, connect it to Wi-Fi and plug it into the wall for power. And that’s it!

So how do you turn your old device into a security camera?

There are a few “free security camera” apps I’ve tried over the years, but some were too difficult to use or not really free. I eventually found Alfred Camera, which I think is the best all-around choice. And yes, I use it in my own home. While there’s a premium (read: paid) option with extra features starting around $36 per year, you can get a lot out of the free, ad-supported version.

Here’s how to set it up

  1. Download Alfred Camera from the App Store (iOS) or Google Play (Android). Do this on both your everyday phone (or tablet) and your old one.
  2. Create a free account.
  3. You will be prompted to upgrade to a paid version, but you can close this screen (tap “X” or “Skip”) and still use the app. (You will be asked this question again in the future.)
  4. Now log in to the same account on both your old and new phone or tablet. Alternatively, you can use your other device to scan the QR code shown on the app, to link the two.
  5. Place the old device in the room you want the camera. From the app’s main menu, find the pull-down menu that lets you use this phone or tablet as the “Camera” or “Viewer.” Select “Camera.”
  6. If you want, rename your camera based on what room it’s in (i.e., “Kids Playroom”).
  7. Finally, on your everyday device, ensure you select “Viewer” from the pull-down menu. You will instantly see what your other phone or tablet sees. On the device that serves as the “Camera,” you can even choose to be notified if it senses sound or movement.
  8. If you want to hook up more than one camera, follow the same process on other old devices. Give each camera a different name. (Note: You are allowed only two online cameras as part of the free tier.)

If you want to see your camera feed from a desktop computer, use the Alfred Camera WebViewer. And yes, it’s free too!

Does this work with all old phones and tablets?

Pretty much! As long as you can download the app, it works with all makes and models of older phones and tablets.

Are there any limitations to the free version?

Yes. Aside from the fact that you will see ads in the free version, there are also a few restrictions:

  • You can’t view your recorded videos inside the app. On the “Viewer” device (presumably the one you use every day), tap Events, and then download the video files to your phone’s external storage to watch them.
  • Your live feed will be in standard definition, not high definition. It should still be good enough, though.
  • There’s less nuance with notifications. The free version gives you “all motion” (or sound) alerts, but the premium tier has AI that can distinguish between a person, pet or vehicle. You also cannot set custom “detection zones” in the free version; this feature lets you draw a virtual boundary box over your camera’s live view to monitor only a specific area.
  • Cameras are limited. As previously mentioned, the free version limits you to two online cameras and one viewer.

But hey, free is free!

Buying an indoor Wi-Fi security camera could cost you anywhere from $25 to $150. And beyond that, there are the cloud service fees for recording and accessing the footage, which could run you $40 to $200 per year. So, yes, this old-device trick is quite the deal.

Plus, there’s something to consider about “free” apps: They are usually monetized in other ways. It could be advertisements, but also check to see if an app is using or sharing your data in any way. Sanchez-Rola says to start with the app store itself. On Apple devices, go to the app you’re interested in and look at “App Privacy” to see what it says; on Android, check “Data safety.” Sanchez-Rola says to “skim the privacy policy for terms like advertising, tracking, sharing and third parties. Think of the privacy label as the nutrition label, and the privacy policy as the ingredients list. Check both.”

Just remember that these disclosures are based on information provided by the developer. “They’re useful,” says Sanchez-Rola, “but they’re not an independent audit of everything the app is doing.”

articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Skip the Small Talk and Get Right to the Point?
articles.content:
I consider myself a small-talk connoisseur. We moved a lot when I was a kid, so I had to get good at connecting with strangers quickly or else no one would have shown up to my birthday parties. Now, as an adult, I’m always down to discuss road construction, light news and even the weather (honestly, there’s so much to say about it these days!). Of course, there are times when small talk gets stuck in the “How are you? I’m fine. How are you?” death spiral, but I’d argue that’s just small talk done badly. Not everyone agrees with me—in fact, some people are even calling for the end of small talk, saying that it can be impersonal, a waste of time and even rude.
So I decided to spend a whole day skipping small talk and just opening with whatever deep conversation topic was on my mind. Here’s how it went:
Read on to discover how my little experiment went and find out if it’s really rude to skip small talk these days.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, relationships, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
My experiment went … surprisingly OK. I thought people would be taken aback by the abruptness—and maybe they were—but they all engaged. The testosterone count was good, the taro chips were delicious (the cashier and I decided to open the bag and try them together, and they have an aftertaste like Froot Loops), my husband still loves me, and the friendly acquaintance is now closer to a friend because we had a great discussion. My daughter did not agree and said slick-backs are a “classic,” calling out portraits from the 1800s, which is actually a good point.
So maybe the anti–small talk crowd is onto something. This approach is more efficient and clear, and there are so many meaty things to discuss in the world, so why not just get to it?
This preference for just getting to the point may be a cultural shift that’s happening right now. A large majority of Gen Zers in the workforce reported feeling comfortable talking about traditionally taboo topics like job satisfaction and pay with colleagues, according to a recent Adobe Future Workforce Study. And my personal experience with the younger crowd is that this isn’t limited to just workplace conversations—an openness I find refreshing. And hey, I’d rather talk about a stranger’s therapy session than deal with a silent Gen Z stare.

  • To a cashier at Costco: “Do you think Lay’s is going too far with selling this 2-pound bag of chili-lime taro chips? That seems like a bold move to go straight to the bulk size when most people couldn’t identify taro on a produce chart.”
  • To my husband: “The fact that the dishes are in the sink and not the dishwasher makes me wonder if you truly love me, and now I’m questioning our relationship.”
  • To my daughter: “Severely parted, slicked-back ponytails are going to be the big thing your generation cringes at when they look back on their teen years. After ‘6-7,’ of course.”
  • To a friendly acquaintance: “I watched a YouTube essay about why Gen Zers aren’t having kids, and I keep thinking about it. Do you think your kids are planning on having children?” (Her kids are 4 and 8.)
  • To a newish work colleague: “I ate a breakfast sandwich one week past its expiration date this morning. Not sure that was the wisest choice.”

Read on to discover how my little experiment went and find out if it’s really rude to skip small talk these days.

  • Relationship: If the person is a complete stranger, like a grocery bagger, then small talk really is the best option because you don’t know anything about them and likely won’t have further interaction.   • Allow the other person to talk. Skipping small talk isn’t an excuse to monologue at someone.

Skipping small talk isn’t inherently rude.
